papers.title: A Multimodal LLM Framework for Short-Term Footfall Time Series Forecasting
papers.abstract: Short-term footfall forecasting is important for staffing, crowd management, energy scheduling, and event-aware operations in large commercial areas. However, this task remains challenging because pedestrian flow is affected by heterogeneous external factors, strong periodic patterns, and abrupt local deviations. Existing forecasting methods often struggle to jointly model multimodal signals and maintain interpretability under high-frequency prediction settings. To address these challenges, this paper proposes MFF-LLM, a multimodal LLM-based forecasting framework with an offline–online design. In the offline stage, aligned observations are transformed into modality-specific token streams. In the online stage, these tokens are processed by a dual-path forecasting network that integrates Stage-1 fusion, a frozen Transformer backbone, explicit modality posterior estimation, history-guided routing, and a two-stage prediction head. Experiments on real-world footfall forecasting show that the MFF-LLM family achieves the strongest and most consistent MAE performance across multiple forecast horizons. Further ablation and mechanism analyses show that the seasonal prior, explicit modality branch, and structured multimodal fusion are key contributors to the final performance. Case studies also demonstrate that the proposed model can follow event-day deviations, preserve major peak–valley patterns, and capture short-term dynamic changes with reasonable fidelity. These results indicate that MFF-LLM provides an effective and interpretable solution for short-term multimodal footfall forecasting.

papers.title: A universal gating framework for multi-expert fusion in heterogeneous multimodal time series forecasting
The Evolution of Financial Time Series Forecasting: From Classical Econometrics to Temporal Foundation Models and Multimodal LLMs
papers.abstract: Financial time series forecasting sits at the intersection of applied mathematics, econometrics, and machine learning. The data generating processes involved are characterized by non-stationarity, regime-dependent volatility clustering, very low signal-to-noise ratios, and reflexive feedback between market participants and asset prices. Over roughly six decades, the dominant methodology has moved through five recognizable phases: classical linear econometrics (ARMA, ARIMA, regularized VAR, VECM), conditional volatility modeling (ARCH/GARCH families, Stochastic Volatility), recursive online signal processing (LMS, RLS, Kalman filters), deep sequence learning (LSTMs, TCNs, patch-based Transformers, State Space Models), and the contemporary period (2024--2026) of Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs), Temporal Language Models (TLMs), and LLMs adapted for financial reasoning. For the purposes of the comparative analysis in Section~10, the deep learning phase is split into two paradigms (recurrent/convolutional networks and Transformer-based architectures), and the foundation model phase is similarly split into numerical TSFMs and multimodal LLM adapters, yielding seven paradigm entries in total. This paper traces that trajectory through the lens of what we call the Capacity-Adaptability Trilemma, a three-way tension between representational capacity, online adaptability, and structural interpretability. We also examine where foundation models fall short in financial contexts, documenting how benchmark contamination and architectural mismatches can cause large zero-shot models to underperform simple statistical baselines. To address this, we propose Econometrically-Informed Neural Networks (EINNs) as a way to embed econometric constraints into modern deep architectures. We present four self-contained synthetic experiments conducted on a MacBook Air M1. These provide limited empirical illustration of several paper claims: that model class rankings shift with SNR and nonlinearity structure (consistent with the trilemma framing), that a noise-dependent crossover exists between DLinear and PatchTST, that trained autoregressors do not beat naive persistence on synthetic random walks, and that the proposed VECM regularizer improves spread stationarity in a bivariate cointegrated setup.

Optimal Text-Based Time-Series Indices
paper.abstract: We propose an approach to construct text-based time-series indices in an optimal way—typically, indices that maximize the contemporaneous relation or the predictive performance with respect to a target variable, such as inflation. Our methodology relies on binary selection matrices that, applied to the vocabulary of tokens, select the relevant texts in the corpus. Various widely known text-based indices, such as the Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index, can be formulated in terms of selection matrices. We design a genetic algorithm with domain-specific knowledge featuring tailor-made crossover and mutation operations to perform the complex optimization. We illustrate our methodology with a corpus of news articles from the Wall Street Journal by optimizing text-based indices that forecast inflation at various horizons.
